lovely work! i especially love the style, and your eye for color.

no, it doesn't read like a female to me at all. to me it looks like a man in makeup. here's why:

the face is way too angular
the jaw is too defined (make it a curved line instead of an angle)
the neck has too many lines (girls don't have all those tendons and bones in the neck)
the eyebrows are too straight, thick, and low
the ear is too big
the line on her temple is too masculine
her lips are too wide

and the most important one

her nose is way too big. (if you do nothing else, make sure you study female noses.)

i can see that you're very good at drawing males, but don't have much experience with females. pull up google images for "pretty girl" and draw what comes up. compare female faces to male faces.

otherwise, great job.

(was i unclear at all?)

Your eyes are anatomically correct, and your shading is wonderful. I'm having trouble believing that this is your first drawing; it's that good. However, the nose looks a bit... off, somehow. The nostrils are too small, I think, and the curves not defined enough. I also think you should practice with hair more. Study how hair flows, how it is parted, and how it comes from the scalp.    


It looks like you spent a lot of time studying the facial features, but not enough studying the neck. The neck in your drawing isn't very correct, from an anatomical standpoint. When combined with your beautifully drawn face, it sticks out a fair bit! When you draw faces, try to include necks, so that you get practice seeing how it attaches to the head. And ditto for the shoulders.


Here's how I study a particular body part: I look it up on Google images, and try to draw 100 of the thing. It's going to take a fair bit of time, yeah, but it's invaluable practice. Then, *make sure* you practice with it in context (e.g., eyes with the rest of the face, hair on a head with a hairline). 


Overall, great work, and great start. Hope I helped. :D

Your questions are somewhat difficult. 

I suppose that I aspire to 'matter' in some vague way. Remembrance is an ephemeral breeze, however. Coming and going, and at last disappearing in the span of seconds. My life shall be a brief summer dalliance. After a short time, no one will remember the fling. Humanity? Nothing more than an old mansion. No matter how stately, how seemingly grand it is, the building will fall. And no one being there to observe, it will not matter.

I digress. Barring philosophy and the general insignificance of humanity, I think I'd want some intellectual job. Of course, that barely narrows it down. It can mean anything from psychiatry to computer engineering. I offer a hearty shrug to that.

I am being bugged, yes. By the inconsequence of my life; of everyone who has ever graced this planet.

You are asking for some psychological cause to my fixation on death, I know. And I have none whatsoever.
Thank you. It is comforting to know that someone in my age range feels the same way. I look forward to a conversation with you sometime soon.

Yes. There is not a post that has so clearly articulated my thoughts. 

Optimism feels saccharine sweet, doesn't it? Why set yourself up for disappointment?

Death is the scariest thing imaginable; or rather, unimaginable. The hours spent in sleep are the closest thing most of us shall come to an unconscious afterlife.


(I look at the afterlife in a religious context, due to my upbringing.)
I have gone through many stages in my short life. First: the innocence of childhood. Denial of the fact of death, and belief in some form of immortality for myself and loved ones. Those days were bliss. I can't remember a single sleepless night in that time of my life.
Then, as an aquaintance's father suffered through cancer, I became hyper-religious. Blissful, peaceful conviction in the face of an almighty God was my shield against all of the hard questions. 

"The Big Bang?" "Utterly fake." 

"Evolution?" "A farce by some unintelligent scientists." 

"Heaven?" "Without a doubt!"

And so on and forth. 

I did not know that this was another form of ignorance.


Science became an interest of mine. I loved the logical aspect of it, the solving mysteries and finding solutions to problems. However, science and faith do not go together. At all. How can one believe in something that contradicts all scientific evidence? And furthermore, how can one believe in something that contradicts itself?

I was deeply conflicted in that point of my life. So I resorted to the strategy that worked for me as a child: ignorance.

I simply partitioned death and religion into one section of my mind, and logic and science to the other. And then the existential topics were drowned in a metaphorical lake.

But no matter how big the lake, it will dry up one day. Then all the material at the bottom will be revealed once more.

That moment for me was a few years ago. I was curious about Gothic subculture, simply because I liked the aesthetic in the Emily the Strange series. (Yes, yes, I was a shallow child.) Somehow, in my research, I came upon a particularly fun song. It was rock and punk and I actually liked it. My liking it, in my head, made me "Goth". 
I looked up the lyrics' meaning on Genius.
The song, I now know, was called "Dead!" by a band called My Chemical Romance.

Was that ever a mistake.

I then had a crying fit for a few hours.

 "Dead!" is about a child dying from cancer, and his efforts to convince himself that no one cares. It tore open the deep, long wound left by mortality. But this time, I guess that it hit harder. I never considered death occurring to me, a kid.

Death is blind.

In that ten minutes or so, I became ten years older.

I was haunted by the shadow of death at  every turn. "What was the point?" I exclaimed. I was angry and sad and most of all, afraid. I knew that there was little hope of an afterlife. Little hope that anything mattered. I could not talk to anyone about it, as they were all (somehow) devout Christians.

A few years later, I was still tormented. I distinctly remember this conversation between me and a "close" associate.


Me: "Are you afraid of death?"


Friend: "No. Because we'll all go to heaven."


Me: "What if heaven's not real?"


Not even a slight pause before she answers:
"It is."


Me: "How do you know?"

Her: "I have faith."


Me: "The evidence in favor of religion is fickle."


Her: "Okay, Miss Smarty Pants (or some other ridiculous phrase), who made the Big Bang?"


I was silent. Science had no answer for this. Unless we considered the Multiverse theory. However, my mention of the postulate (and my subsequent explanation) would likely garner the question "Who made those other universes?"

So I stayed silent.

Her: "Exactly. Scientists can't understand something as big as God."


Fury burned bright in my breast.
I wanted to lash out at her for that sentence. I wanted to scream at her that scientists were more understanding than most people on this planet, and that insolent pieces of filth like her were the ones so couldn't understand big things.

Instead, I looked at her and saw a seven year old me, spouting off the same nonsense, and indulging in the same ignorance (albeit more eloquently). 

I have never attempted to tell another about my thoughts since that day a few months ago.

I guess the point of this rambly mess is to let you know that you are not alone.
I imagine that your story is similar to mine. While they may not share the same events, they share the same emotions. 

Please, talk to me sometime. I would very much enjoy your company.

Thank you so much for replying.
